summary:
Anguilla is a British Overseas Territory whose law is local law: the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 and its 2025 single-sex-services code do not automatically extend to the island, and they can be applied there only by Order in Council.

Sex between men in private is legal, but the repeal was imposed from London rather than enacted by Anguilla's own legislature. On 5 January 2001 the Privy Council ordered decriminalisation of private consensual same-sex conduct in five Caribbean territories — Anguilla, the Cayman Islands, the British Virgin Islands, Montserrat and the Turks and Caicos Islands — acting unilaterally after the local legislatures refused to repeal their statutes, and religious leaders protested the decision. Anguilla had never carried the prohibition in exactly the same statutory form as those other territories. A first-person account published in June 2023 dates the change to 2000 rather than January 2001.

Same-sex marriage is not recognised under Anguilla law. A commercial destination-wedding service states that plainly while marketing the island's venues to same-sex couples, which means a ceremony performed there carries symbolic status only.

Public LGBT life on the island is close to invisible: no community organisations, no venues, no Pride, and only a handful of hotels marketed to gay travellers. Anguilla's roughly 15,000 residents and 35 square miles are given as reasons the scene stays small, and the muted, not 'out and proud' atmosphere is attributed to the imposed colonial legacy rather than to local choice. A queer family visiting in June 2023 described the trip as uneventful.
tangentialFactors:
Anguilla's decriminalisation was part of a single sweep across five British Caribbean territories decided by the same court on the same day, so the pattern of externally imposed reform, and the religious protest that followed it, is regional rather than peculiar to this island.

The gap between law and marketing is visible in the wedding trade: vendors promote ceremonies for same-sex couples on the island while acknowledging in the same material that the law does not recognise those marriages.

Comparatively, Anguilla sits at the end of a spectrum in which decriminalisation is settled but relationship recognition is absent, and where the absence of any organised local LGBT presence means visitors encounter neither hostility campaigns nor visible support infrastructure.
localsOnly:
Residents live under ultimate United Kingdom legal authority, so changes to the framework governing sexual conduct and equality arrive by Order in Council rather than through the local legislature, whose members declined to repeal the former prohibition themselves.

Same-sex couples resident in Anguilla cannot marry, and there is no local organisation, venue or annual event through which residents might press for a change; the island's small population is itself cited as a reason no such scene exists.

Religious leaders on the island objected when the decriminalisation order came down from London, and that objection is part of the local political memory surrounding the issue.

Residents seeking protections of the kind the United Kingdom's Equality Act 2010 provides must rely on Anguilla's own statutes, since the national measure has not been extended locally.
outOfScopeNotes:
The inventory does not contain the text of the instrument by which decriminalisation took effect in Anguilla, so the precise statutory mechanism and its current wording are unresolved here.

Sources disagree on the date of the change: a 2023 travel account gives 2000, while the contemporaneous Associated Press report of the Privy Council order is dated 5 January 2001. Both are reported as sourced; the discrepancy is unresolved.

Whether the Equality Act 2010 or the 2025 single-sex-services code has ever been the subject of an Order in Council extending it to Anguilla is not sourced in this inventory and remains unresolved.

No sourced material in this inventory addresses gender recognition, identity-document marker rules, hate-crime or hate-speech protection, access to gender-affirming care, or screening procedures at entry that could disclose a visitor's trans status. These are not established either way by the available sources.

The claim that Anguilla never had the prohibition in the same statutory form as the other territories rests on a single 2012 country report and is not corroborated against primary legal text in this inventory.
